stimulus.text:
“I long to hear that you have declared an independency — and by the way in the new Code of Laws which I suppose it will be necessary for you to make I desire you would Remember the Ladies, and be more generous and favourable to them than your ancestors. Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of the Husbands. Remember all Men would be tyrants if they could. If perticuliar care and attention is not paid to the Laidies we are determined to foment a Rebelion, and will not hold ourselves bound by any Laws in which we have no voice, or Representation.”
— Abigail Adams to John Adams, Braintree, March 31, 1776 (abridged; spelling as in the original)
stimulus.source_note: Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776, public domain.

books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals, B. Evolving Ideas on Gender

stem: The letter is most significant as evidence that the Revolution's ideals

options.text: Were written to free enslaved people and to give women the vote
options.misconception: Neither happened; the Declaration's words were about independence from Britain, and neither group gained those rights in the 1770s.

options.text: Applied only to white men who owned property
options.misconception: The ideals were claimed far more widely than that, by women, free Black people, and enslaved people; the letter itself proves the claim spread.

options.text: Were claimed by people its leaders never meant to include, and went unanswered
Were rejected by women, who preferred the old legal order
options.misconception: Adams and other women pressed for change; the letter is a demand, not a defense of the old order.

rationales.C: Adams uses the Revolution's own language of liberty and representation to claim a place for women. Background: her husband's reply laughs the request off, and married women's legal standing barely changed for decades.
rationales.A: The ideals were written about independence, not about freeing enslaved people or giving women the vote.
rationales.B: The letter shows the ideals reaching beyond property owners, since a woman claims them for wives.
rationales.D: Women did not reject the ideals; Adams uses them to demand a better standing for wives.
rationales.general:
1. Watch the language travel. Adams takes the Patriots' words — liberty, representation — and aims them at husbands.
2. Watch the answer. Background: her husband's reply laughs the request off and keeps the “masculine systems” in place.
3. Judge the pattern. Background: her letter is one of many claims the ideals inspired that the new republic did not grant.
Remember: an ideal's reach is measured by who claims it, not only by who wrote it.
